opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot. Proving theorems is, in some sense, the more tractable half of the problem. If you give a system a well-posed statement, especially in a formal language like Lean, there is a clear signal: the proof either checks or it doesn't. That verifiability is what makes reinforcement learning and search work so well there.

Posing good questions is much harder, because there's no compiler for "interesting." What makes a conjecture good? It should be true, or at least plausibly true. It shouldn't be trivial, and it shouldn't be hopelessly out of reach. Ideally it connects to things mathematicians already care about, and solving it should open doors rather than close off a dead end. Human mathematicians develop that taste over years: reading papers, talking to advisors, failing on problems, noticing patterns across fields. A lot of it is tacit knowledge.

So how might an AI get there? A few thoughts.

First, I think proving and conjecturing aren't separate. When a system proves many things, it accumulates lemmas, definitions, and techniques, and it can start to see which intermediate results get reused, which concepts compress a lot of mathematics, and which questions sit at the frontier of what it can do. That's a kind of self-generated curriculum. If you have a strong prover, you can use it as a critic for a conjecture generator: propose, attempt, learn which proposals were productive.

Second, formal verification gives you a grounding that informal models lack. One danger with language models generating math is that they produce things that sound deep but are wrong or vacuous. If conjectures live in a formal system, you can at least filter out the false and the trivial automatically, and focus the scarce human judgment on what's actually interesting.

Third, I do think humans stay in the loop for a long time on the question of taste. Mathematics is a human endeavor in the sense that what counts as important is partly a community judgment. I don't see AI replacing that. I see it as a collaborator that can explore far more examples, test far more hypotheses, and surface patterns a person might never notice, and then mathematicians decide what's beautiful.

And historically, intuition often comes from computation and examples. Gauss computed tables of primes before conjecturing the prime number theorem. Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer came out of computer experiments. If AI can do that kind of exploration at massive scale, and couple it with rigorous verification, I think we can get something that starts to look like intuition. Not identical to human intuition, but genuinely useful for discovery.

So I'm optimistic, but I'd say it's the deepest open problem in the field, more than the proving itself.

fable-5.1.text:
I think this is actually the hardest and most interesting part of the whole AI for Math question, and it's where I'd push back a little on how people usually frame progress.

Most of the benchmarks we talk about, whether it's IMO problems or formalizing theorems in Lean, are fundamentally about answering. Someone hands you a well-posed question, there's a known answer or at least a known target, and the model's job is to get there. That's a solver. And solvers have gotten remarkably good, faster than I expected honestly. But if you look at how mathematics actually advances, the solving step is often not the bottleneck. The bottleneck is deciding what's worth solving.

When I was doing research math, the moments that mattered were almost never "I found the proof." They were "wait, this object looks like it wants to be that object" or "this special case is suspiciously clean, there must be a general statement here." That's intuition, and it's really a kind of taste. You have thousands of possible directions, almost all of them are either trivial or hopeless, and a good mathematician has this sense for the narrow band of problems that are hard enough to be interesting and tractable enough to actually make progress on. Nobody ever writes that down explicitly. It's learned by apprenticeship, by watching your advisor get excited about one thing and bored by another.

So the challenge for AI is that there's no clean training signal for taste. You can verify a proof. You can't easily verify that a conjecture is "good." A conjecture is good partly because of what it would unlock, which depends on the whole structure of the field, and partly because of a kind of aesthetic judgment that's hard to make rigorous. If you just reward models for generating true statements, you get an avalanche of true, boring statements. The space of valid theorems is enormous and almost all of it is noise.

What I find hopeful is a few things. One is that intuition in math is not magic, it's pattern recognition across a lot of examples, and that's something these systems are structurally good at. A model that has read the whole literature might actually notice analogies between distant areas that no single human would see, because no human has that breadth. Two, there's a loop you can build where the solver gives you feedback on the question-asker. If a model proposes a conjecture and then a solver finds it's trivially true, or trivially false, or completely stuck, that's signal about whether the question was well-calibrated. Formal systems like Lean give you that kind of grounded feedback at scale, which humans never had.

But I'd be honest that I don't think we're there yet, and I'm a little skeptical of anyone who says a model has "mathematical intuition" today. What we have are very strong solvers that occasionally surprise you with a clever step. The creator part, the thing that wakes up with a new question it genuinely wants to understand, I think that requires something we haven't quite figured out how to train for. And it might require letting these systems work on open problems for a long time and fail a lot, which is how humans develop taste too. That's uncomfortable because it's expensive and the metrics are fuzzy. But I think it's the real frontier.

astra-6.text:
I think posing good questions is a much harder target than solving a given problem, because it’s not obvious what the reward should be. If you give a system a mathematical statement, you can ask whether its proof is correct. But if you ask it to propose a new statement, correctness alone isn’t enough. It could generate infinitely many true statements that nobody finds interesting.

So the challenge is: can it recognize what’s worth understanding? A good question might connect two areas, expose a missing assumption, or turn a collection of examples into a general principle. And sometimes a very good question looks small initially; its importance only becomes clear after you work on it.

I think mathematical intuition is closely tied to that process. You explore examples, look for patterns, try an argument, and discover why it fails. That failure can tell you that you’ve formulated the wrong conjecture—or that there’s a more interesting phenomenon underneath it. I’d want an AI system to participate in that whole loop, including revising the question.

A practical starting point would be collaboration with mathematicians: can the system suggest an example or a conjecture that changes how someone thinks about a problem? That’s a more concrete test of creative usefulness. Producing something new is one thing; producing something that opens up productive mathematical work is the real challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s one of the deepest challenges in AI for math. Solving a problem gives you a relatively clear objective: you have a statement, and you want a proof. Asking a good question is much harder to evaluate. A question can be difficult without being interesting, and it can be simple but reveal something fundamental.

To me, mathematical intuition includes knowing which examples to examine, which patterns might generalize, and when a failed approach is telling you to change the question. So I’d want an AI to participate in that whole process: explore examples, propose a conjecture, look for counterexamples, and revise its understanding.

The challenge is that checking a proof doesn’t tell you whether the theorem was worth discovering. We need ways to recognize questions that connect ideas or open up productive directions. I think collaboration with mathematicians will be especially valuable there—seeing whether an AI’s questions actually help people develop new mathematics.
